title: This earthly tent (2 Corinthians 5:1–10)
hookLine: our body a tent; a house not made with hands
carry: a house not made with hands
tomorrow: two people dodge each other in the cereal aisle. who goes first?

cards: Rain on a tent at night. The rasp of the zipper, the cold coming up through the floor, the poles creaking when the wind leans on them. A tent is a real home, and it never lets you forget it's a temporary one.

Paul knew tents. Acts says that in Corinth he worked with Aquila and Priscilla, "for by their occupation they were tentmakers." So when he wants a word for the human body, he reaches for one from his own workbench.

teach.h: A TENT, AND A BUILDING OF GOD.
teach.b: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." Tabernacle here means a tent.
And Paul doesn't call the tent worthless. You sleep in it, you get rained on in it.
He says we groan in it, burdened, a word that fits a long illness or a tired back. Then the turn.
He doesn't long to be unclothed, but clothed upon, "that mortality might be swallowed up of life." The hope isn't less life. It's more.
In between comes a line the King James sets in brackets, almost an aside: "(For we walk by faith, not by sight:)".

teach.h: WHAT'S DONE IN THE BODY COUNTS.
teach.b: Then something sober: all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, to receive for what was done in the body. So the tent matters. What happens in it counts.

teach.h: A HOUSE NOT MADE WITH HANDS.
teach.b: Christians read the house not made with hands in more than one way: some as the resurrection body to come, some as being at home with the Lord.
One to tell a friend tonight: a man who stitched tents for a living calls the body a tent, and still calls it a house. The passage holds the hope without drawing the floor plan.

how: Some churches read 2 Corinthians 5:1 at funerals, and some Christians keep 'we walk by faith, not by sight' as a line for hard seasons of illness or age.

s: Paul calls the body a worthless cage to escape

games.q: your aunt, after a long illness, says she feels 'trapped in a broken body.' what does Paul's picture offer her?
o: the body is a real home that groans, and the hope is more life, not less.
the body is a cage, and she should be glad to be rid of it soon.
if her faith were stronger, her body wouldn't be failing like this.
games.why: Paul doesn't call the tent worthless. we groan, burdened, and long to be clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.

practice: Stand, if you can, and walk slowly across the room and back; if you can't right now, press your feet into the floor instead. Feel the tent at work: heels, knees, the hinge of the hips, the breath filling and leaving.
Then rest a hand on one part that's tired, and thank it.

wordCard.voice: This earthly tent. Paul's picture of the body: a real home, groaned in and mended, waiting for a house not made with hands.

orig.note: Greek: a tent; the 'tabernacle' of 2 Corinthians 5:1 and 5:4.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: a house not made with hands, and a tent worth caring for until then. Good night.
